summary: Explains why IPsec and Network Address Translation (NAT) often do not work together, and lists requirements for fixing the problems. The motivation is practical: VPNs are widely used by telecommuters, but NATs in home gateways and hotels get in the way. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Home routers rewrite addresses on packets, but a secure tunnel checks that nothing was changed. This note lists how those two clash and what must be fixed.

questions: why does ipsec not work with nat
why does ah not work through nat
what are the requirements for ipsec nat traversal
subtitle: Why NAT breaks IPsec in so many ways, and what a fix has to achieve.

tldr.problem: IPsec is widely used for VPNs and telecommuter access, but NATs in home gateways and hotels change addresses and ports in ways that break IPsec and IKE.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC catalogues sixteen known incompatibilities in three groups, then lists criteria that any IPsec-NAT compatibility solution must meet, and reviews IPsec tunnel mode, RSIP and 6to4 against them.
tldr.outcome: It is a requirements document used to evaluate protocol submissions, not a protocol. It concludes that AH and NAT are fundamentally incompatible, so a solution need not support AH.

today: RFC 3715 is an Informational requirements document and the data does not list it as obsoleted or updated. It frames the problem and the criteria for solutions rather than defining a protocol.

sections.title: The Telecommuter Problem
sections.content:
Perhaps the most common use of IPsec is virtual private networking (VPN), and a very popular VPN use is giving telecommuters access to the corporate Intranet. Meanwhile NATs are widely deployed in home gateways and in places such as hotels. The RFC says the resulting IPsec-NAT incompatibilities have become a major barrier to deploying IPsec in one of its principal uses.

The requirements are meant for evaluating protocol submissions. A submission is not compliant if it fails any MUST or MUST NOT requirement for the capabilities it implements, and is called unconditionally compliant only if it also meets all SHOULD and SHOULD NOT requirements.
sections.eli5: People working from home want a private tunnel to their office, but the box in their home that shares the internet keeps tripping it up.

sections.title: Known Incompatibilities
sections.content:
The RFC lists sixteen problems, labelled a) to p), in three categories: intrinsic NA(P)T issues, implementation weaknesses that many NATs share, and problems caused by NAT "helper" features.

Key intrinsic issues:

  • AH covers the IP addresses in its integrity check, so any address change invalidates it. ESP does not cover them.
  • Checksums: TCP and UDP checksums include a pseudo-header with the addresses, so a NAT invalidates them where they are checked. SCTP uses a CRC32C that does not cover the IP header, so it is unaffected.
  • IKE identifiers: if IP addresses are used as identifiers, translation causes a mismatch and IKE implementations are required to discard such packets.
  • Ports and SPIs: multiple hosts behind a NAPT need the IKE source port translated, so responders must accept a UDP source port other than 500. ESP traffic is opaque, so the NAT demultiplexes on destination address, protocol and SPI, and two hosts may choose the same SPI.
  • Embedded addresses inside protected payloads cannot be translated, defeating ALGs in the NAT, and NAT directionality prevents unsolicited IPsec SAs to hosts behind it.

Implementation weaknesses include NATs that cannot handle non-UDP/TCP traffic such as ESP (protocol 50) or AH (protocol 51), mapping timeouts, and poor handling of fragments. Helper problems include inspecting ISAKMP cookies and payloads, and not translating packets with UDP source port 500.
sections.eli5: The secure tunnel puts a seal on the letter, and the home router sometimes has to change the address on the envelope. If the seal also covers the address, changing it breaks the seal.

sections.title: Requirements for a Solution
sections.content:
Because IPv6 would address the address scarcity behind NAT, the RFC treats IPsec-NAT compatibility as a transitional problem. A solution MUST be deployable on a shorter time scale than IPv6 and SHOULD require changes only to hosts, not routers or NATs.

  • Scenarios: it MUST support the telecommuter case (tunnel mode, or L2TP over IPsec transport mode, through more than one NAT) and host-to-host communication, and the gateway-to-gateway case is described.
  • Firewalls: administrators MUST be able to write simple static rules for IKE and IPsec traversal, so dynamic port allocation is to be avoided.
  • Scaling: it must work with thousands of telecommuters, and MUST address overlapping SPD entries and demultiplexing of incoming packets.
  • Modes: gateways MUST support ESP tunnel mode and hosts IPsec transport mode. Because NAT and AH are fundamentally incompatible, AH support is not required.
  • Compatibility: it MUST interoperate with existing IKE and IPsec implementations and SHOULD detect whether a NAT is present. It MUST NOT introduce new IKE or IPsec vulnerabilities, and IKE MUST be able to re-key in both directions.
sections.eli5: A good fix must work with what people already own, keep doors locked against strangers, and cope with thousands of home workers.

sections.title: Existing Approaches
sections.content:
The RFC reviews three existing approaches. IPsec tunnel mode can traverse a NAT in a limited set of circumstances: ESP is used, there is no address validation, "any to any" SPD entries are negotiated, only a single client sits behind the NAT, fragmentation is avoided, and sessions stay active. Those conditions are too limited, so a more general solution is needed.

RSIP handles SPI demultiplexing and SPD overlap and works with embedded addresses, but needs an RSIP-enabled gateway, and the RFC judges that it solves a transitional problem on a long-term time scale, which is not useful. 6to4 can work well where a single NAT separates client and VPN gateway, but it needs a routable IPv4 address on the NAT, does not work through multiple NATs, and requires NAT changes.
sections.eli5: Three existing tricks each work in some homes but not others, so none is the full answer.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An IPsec-NAT solution means hosts must securely process packets whose IP headers are not cryptographically protected. Since AH cannot pass through a NAT, ESP with null encryption may be used instead, but it does not give the same protection. The RFC gives IPv6 source routing risks as an example that AH precludes and ESP with null encryption does not.

ESP does not protect against source address spoofing, so the anti-spoofing check on the source address matters. The RFC's example has hosts A and C behind different NATs with tunnels to router B. If C spoofs A's address and no check ties the address to the SPI, C could gain A's privileges. Therefore an IPsec-NAT scheme MUST provide some degree of anti-spoofing protection.
sections.eli5: If nobody checks who a visitor really is, one person could pretend to be someone more important and get into rooms they should not.

viz.caption: THE THREE EXISTING APPROACHES AS THE RFC ASSESSES THEM

cells: Can traverse a NAT in limited circumstances
Needs ESP, a single client and other restrictive conditions
Solves SPI demultiplexing and SPD overlap
Needs an RSIP-enabled gateway; transitional problem on a long-term time scale
Robust with a single NAT between client and gateway
Needs a routable IPv4 address on the NAT and NAT changes
